newsitem.title: USA: Nobel winners fear "decay" in U.S. science.
newsitem.headline: Nobel winners fear "decay" in U.S. science.

text.p: Five new U.S. Nobel science prize winners Thursday outlined a gloomy picture of a decay in basic U.S. science that could threaten human progress on a crowded 21st century Earth.

"The process is in a state of decay right now," said Richard Smalley of Rice University in Houston, co-winner of this year's Chemistry prize for discovering the "buckyball," a new form of the element carbon.
The harmful repercussions of this "invidious" undermining of basic research would not be seen for some years, he told a news conference sponsored by the National Science Foundation.

As the Earth's population swells, perhaps doubling to 12 billion people by the middle of the next century, advances in technology, renewable energy, materials and agriculture will be imperative. But the foundations have to come from basic science now, the laureates said.
There is often a lag of years or decades between a basic scientific discovery and applied development.

According to an analysis by the American Association for the Advancement of Science, funding for non-defence research and development will drop in constant dollars by up to 23 percent by the year 2002, depending on how the current balanced budget battles turn out in Congress.

At the same time, the five Nobel laureates in physics and chemistry said, big corporations with pioneering laboratories that once propelled scientific discovery have pulled back, unable to count on making the investment in basic research pay off in the long-run.

After the Second World War and the dawn of the nuclear age, and the start of the Cold War-era space race with the Soviet Union, "the U.S. supported science almost as a religion," said Douglas Osheroff, a Stanford University physicist who won the prize this year for his work on superfluidity.
The five scientists said that many things people take for granted today, such as computers, lasers and semi-conductors, evolved out of basic discoveries a generation or more ago.

Robert Richardson, from Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., a co-winner of this year's Physics prize, lamented what he called the "abysmal" state of science education in the United States, as well as ignorance about mathematics and science on the part of many lawmakers and policymakers.
In this presidential election year, he said, he hears little public discussion about national science goals and priorities.
"It is not near the top of the national consciousness," he said.
